name: Emeka Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Emeka, thanks for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and this conversation is confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the discount supermarket by the bus station, the one where everything's sold out of the cardboard boxes. We sit down at the tills and you're meant to scan fast, there's a number on the screen that tells you your items per minute. Mine's not great, I'm still one of the slowest. When it's quiet they send me to break down boxes and fill the middle aisle with whatever random stuff is on offer that week, drills, paddling pools, that kind of thing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's simple, I know what I'm doing each day, and I like that. The grind is the speed number and the contract, which is twenty-four hours a week, and you take extra shifts when they're offered. Some weeks I get thirty-five hours, some weeks twenty-four, and you can't plan anything around that.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room above a barber's on Mill Street, I share a kitchen with two other guys. Five-a-side on Tuesdays, that's my thing. I don't use any of the AI stuff, my phone's for football and messages, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Fine by me, I never trusted it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, it was just a lot of talk. At five-a-side we'd have a laugh about it. I don't really post online, so that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing gets better either. The problem was always my hours, not robots. If they cut me back to twenty-four for a few months, I'm short on rent, simple as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and say yes to every extra shift going. I'd stop eating out after football, which is about fifteen a week. And maybe ask my cousin about labouring work on his building sites on my days off, if he's got any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, a bit. It's not the AI, it's the rent, it's always the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How close are you to not making rent right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got maybe two weeks of money if nothing goes wrong. Last month my phone screen broke and I had to borrow sixty from my mum. I hate doing that, she's got her own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there other shop jobs in town if this one went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not many. There's the big supermarket out of town, but you need a car, and the corner shops are family-run, they hire their own. So I hold on to this one.

say: AI was **just talk**, like I said all along.
We'd have a **laugh** about it at five-a-side; I don't post online.
think: The problem was always my **hours**, not robots.
A few months on **twenty-four hours** and I'm **short** on rent.
do: Say yes to every **extra shift** going.
Stop **eating out** after football, saving about fifteen a week.
Ask his cousin about **labouring work** on days off.
feel: **Tight** in the chest over the **rent**, not over AI.
S0.quote: The problem was always my hours, not robots.
fieldNote: Already living on **two weeks** of money; borrowed sixty from his mum for a phone screen.
His **flexible contract** is the real threat in a world where AI changes little.
Few nearby options: the other supermarket needs a **car** he doesn't have.

steps.text: Take every extra till shift the store offers
Stop eating out after Tuesday football
Ask his cousin for building site labouring on days off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking jobs. Okay. That's not me, I scan beans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem this time. At work we'd say good luck to head office. I'd keep out of arguments about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But actually, I reckon it's head office that sets my hours, and if their computer gets cleverer it'll just cut them finer. It already knows when the shop's quiet. If it decides Tuesday mornings need two tills not three, that's me sent home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, I'm not going to learn computers, that's not me. I'd ask my cousin for more regular labouring work, maybe one day a week, so I'm not stuck if hours drop. I'd cut the phone contract down too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the ref's looking at his watch and you're a goal down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides your hours now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The manager, Mrs Okafor, but she says the system gives her the numbers. She's fair, she tries to share the hours out. If the system gets stricter, she can't help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it's not you, but you also think the system will cut your hours. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. Head office isn't coming for my job, it's coming for my hours. I didn't really think about the difference until you asked.

say: This one's **head office's problem**, not ours.
I **scan beans**, so thinking jobs aren't my worry.
I'd keep out of **arguments** about it at work.
think: A cleverer **computer** at head office will cut my **hours** finer.
If it decides Tuesdays need **two tills**, I'm sent home.
do: Keep working the tills and refuse to **learn computers**.
Get **one day a week** of labouring from his cousin.
Cut his **phone contract** to a cheaper one.
feel: **Uneasy**, like being a **goal down** late in a match.
S1.quote: Head office isn't coming for my job, it's coming for my hours.
fieldNote: Starts by dismissing it, then works out that **scheduling software** hits him directly.
Trusts his manager, **Mrs Okafor**, but sees her as powerless against the system.
Resists learning tech; his backup is **manual labour** through family.

steps.text: Keep scanning on the tills without learning new tech
Arrange one day a week of labouring with his cousin
Switch to a cheaper phone contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And then robots that can do my job by 2031. I don't really know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should stop it. At work everyone would be talking about it and I'd probably just listen. I wouldn't know who to blame, honestly, it's just how business goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished in that shop by 2031, maybe sooner, because they'll use the AI to plan everything and then the robots do the rest. I'd be thirty-one with no skills except scanning and breaking down boxes. I've got two weeks of money, there is no plan for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd move back in with my mum to stop paying rent, even though I'd hate it. I'd go full time on building sites with my cousin if he'd have me, because a robot building a wall seems further off. Then I'd wait, because I don't know what else is worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like I'm standing in the road and I can see the bus but I can't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum when you asked to move back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not forever, just till I find something steady. She'd say yes straight away, that's her. But I'd feel like a kid again at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe driving, a proper licence for vans. But if the AI drives too, what's the point? That's what stops me, I don't know what lasts.

say: I wouldn't know who to **blame**; it's just how business goes.
think: I'm **finished** at the shop by **2031**, maybe sooner.
At thirty-one I'd have **no skills** but scanning and boxes.
do: Move back to his **mum's** to stop paying rent.
Go full time on **building sites** with his cousin.
**Wait**, because he doesn't know what lasts.
feel: **Sick** and **frozen**, like seeing a bus coming and not moving.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-one with no skills except scanning and breaking down boxes.
fieldNote: No plan and no money: **two weeks** of savings and a fear of picking the wrong skill.
Doesn't blame anyone; sees it as **how business goes**.
Moving home to his **mum** feels like failure but is his first step.

steps.text: Move back in with his mum to stop paying rent
Work full time on his cousin's building sites
Hold off on any course until he sees what lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots 2034. A bit more time, but it ends the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that it's mad, but I'd probably say it less. People get used to things. At work we'd joke that we're the last cashiers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have till about 2034 in the shop, which is seven years. That's long enough to do something, but I don't trust myself to pick right. I'd probably do nothing for two years and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing Saturdays on the building sites now, so I've got something by the time it hits. I'd try to save a bit, even twenty a week, in a separate account I can't see. And I'd keep my shop job as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the last one. I can still sleep in this one, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing for two years and then panic. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I did after school, I waited and the good apprenticeships went. I'm not proud of it. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop that happening this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin pushing me, probably. He's the one who always calls me. If he says come Saturday, I'll come.

say: It's still **mad**, but people **get used** to things.
We'd joke at work that we're the **last cashiers**.
think: I'd have till about **2034** in the shop, **seven years**.
I don't trust myself to **pick right**; I'd wait, then panic.
do: Start **Saturdays** on the building sites now.
Save **twenty a week** in a separate account.
Keep the **shop job** as long as they'd have him.
S3.quote: I'd probably do nothing for two years and then panic.
fieldNote: Honest about his own **delay**: he waited after school and missed apprenticeships.
His **cousin** is the push that actually moves him.
Still expects to **lose the shop job**, only later.

steps.text: Work Saturdays on his cousin's building sites
Save twenty a week in a separate account
Keep his till job as long as the store keeps him

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and the robots in 2039. I'd be nearly forty. That feels far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's loads of time and not to worry. At work we'd say it's not our problem yet. Probably the same at five-a-side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd ignore it for years, because ten years feels like forever. But the shop's still going to need fewer of us, and the hours thing from the steady one still happens in the meantime. I'm not going to be a cashier at forty anyway, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shop job and do the odd day labouring like now. Maybe after a few years, I'd look at a proper trade, like plastering, with my cousin's mate. I'd wait and see how it goes in the shops first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit of a knot about money, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the sign that tells you to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put robots in the big supermarket out of town, that's when I'd know it's real. Until then it's just news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if that sign came in, say, 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have two years and I'd be scrambling, I know. I'd have to hope plastering's still a thing. I'd probably wish I'd started earlier.

say: There's **loads of time**, so don't worry.
It's **not our problem** yet at the shop.
At five-a-side we'd say **nearly forty** is a long way off.
think: I'd **ignore it** for years because ten years feels like forever.
Meanwhile fewer staff and **shorter hours** still happen.
do: Keep the **shop job** and odd days of **labouring**.
Look at a **plastering** trade after a few years.
**Wait** for robots at the big out-of-town supermarket as his sign.
S4.quote: If they put robots in the big supermarket out of town, that's when I'd know it's real.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets him **put things off**, which he half admits is a trap.
His trigger to act is seeing **robots locally**, not reading news.
Still faces **hour cuts** from scheduling software in the meantime.

steps.text: Keep the till job and do odd labouring days
Wait for robots at the out-of-town supermarket before acting
Ask his cousin's friend about learning plastering in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing ready and nowhere to go but my mum's. What would help is someone telling me clearly which jobs last, and paying me while I learn one. I'd do an apprenticeship at thirty if it paid rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the contract. Everyone talks about robots but nobody talks about twenty-four-hour contracts. If I had forty guaranteed hours, I could save and none of this would scare me as much.

headlineQuote: If I had forty guaranteed hours, I could save and none of this would scare me as much.
portrait: Emeka is 27, a slow-scanning **till worker** at a discount supermarket, renting a room on Mill Street.
He's on a **twenty-four-hour contract**, has about two weeks of money and avoids **AI tools** entirely.
He sees **hours, not robots**, as the threat, and leans on his **cousin** and mum.
He freezes in the fast AGI picture and **puts things off** when given more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have nothing ready and would end up at his **mum's**.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice on which **jobs last**, and a **paid apprenticeship** that covers rent.
